title: Docker Multi-Stage Builds
summary: A study-notes series on Docker multi-stage builds: how stages, COPY --from and layer caching work, BuildKit cache mounts, minimal final images (alpine, distroless), dev/test targets, ARG scoping, non-root users, .dockerignore and measured image-size savings.

chapters.title: Docker Multi-Stage Builds: Cover
points: Docker: build once, ship a small image — multi-stage builds separate build tools from the runtime
Series map: stages, COPY --from, cache, BuildKit mounts, final images, targets, ARG, security, .dockerignore, cheatsheet
The problem: single-stage images ship compilers, source, package caches and dev dependencies to production
The promise: typical Go/Node/Java images shrink from ~1 GB to 10–200 MB
Prerequisite vocabulary: image, layer, build context, Dockerfile instruction, registry
Running example used throughout: a small web app built in a builder stage and run in a slim stage

chapters.title: Why Multi-Stage: The Single-Stage Problem
points: Definition: a multi-stage Dockerfile has several FROM lines; each FROM starts a new stage with a fresh filesystem
Only the last stage (or the --target stage) becomes the final image; earlier stages are discarded from it
Single-stage: golang:1.22 image is ~800 MB because it holds the toolchain, source and module cache
Old workaround: the 'builder pattern' with two Dockerfiles and a shell script copying artifacts via docker cp
Multi-stage replaces that with one Dockerfile and one docker build command
Smaller image means faster pull, faster deploy, lower registry cost and smaller attack surface
Example: FROM golang:1.22 AS build / RUN go build -o /app ./cmd/server / FROM alpine / COPY --from=build /app /app
Mistake: leaving build tools (gcc, git, npm devDependencies) in the final stage
Mistake: assuming earlier stages are pushed — they stay only in the local build cache
Intermediate stages still cost build time and cache space even though they are not shipped

chapters.title: FROM ... AS Stages and COPY --from
points: FROM image AS name gives a stage a name; without AS, stages are numbered from 0
COPY --from=build /src/out /app copies files from a named stage's filesystem
COPY --from=0 refers to a stage by index — fragile when stages are reordered, prefer names
COPY --from=nginx:1.27 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /tmp/ copies from an external image, not just stages
Stage names are case-insensitive lowercase by convention: build, deps, test, runtime
A stage can start FROM a previous stage: FROM base AS dev reuses its layers and ENV
Only files are copied — ENV, WORKDIR, USER and installed packages from the source stage do not carry over
COPY --from --chown=app:app /app /app sets ownership during the copy
COPY --link (BuildKit) makes the copied layer independent so base changes do not invalidate it
Node example: build stage runs npm ci && npm run build, runtime stage copies only /app/dist and production node_modules
Mistake: copying from a stage that does not exist yields 'invalid from flag value' or 'pull access denied'
Mistake: forgetting that a COPY from a stage copies the whole path, including unwanted build artifacts

chapters.title: Build Cache and Layer Ordering
points: Every RUN, COPY and ADD instruction creates a layer; unchanged layers are reused from cache
Cache key for a layer: the instruction text plus, for COPY/ADD, a checksum of the copied file contents
Once one layer is invalidated, every later layer in that stage is rebuilt
Rule: order instructions from least to most frequently changing
Dependency-first pattern: COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ then RUN npm ci, then COPY . .
Go pattern: COPY go.mod go.sum ./ then RUN go mod download, then COPY . . then RUN go build
Bad ordering: COPY . . before npm ci means any source edit re-installs all dependencies
Combine related commands in one RUN with && and clean caches in the same layer (apt-get update && apt-get install -y x && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
Deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image — the data remains in the earlier layer
Stages are independent in cache: changing the runtime stage does not rebuild the builder stage
BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel and skips stages not needed by the target
Mistake: RUN apt-get update alone in its own layer gets cached and serves stale package lists
docker build --no-cache and --pull force a clean rebuild of layers and base images

chapters.title: BuildKit Cache Mounts and Secrets
points: BuildKit is the default builder in modern Docker; the syntax is enabled with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 on the first line
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci keeps the npm cache between builds without storing it in a layer
Cache mounts persist on the builder host, so a changed lockfile only downloads new packages
Go example: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build go build ./...
pip example: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
apt example: cache /var/cache/apt and /var/lib/apt with sharing=locked to avoid concurrent corruption
Options: id= names a cache, sharing=shared|private|locked controls concurrent access, mode= and uid= set permissions
Cache mounts vs layer cache: layer cache is all-or-nothing per instruction, a cache mount is incremental inside a RUN
RUN --mount=type=bind,source=package.json,target=package.json mounts files without a COPY layer
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc uses a credential at build time without baking it into any layer
Pass the secret with docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .
Mistake: using ARG or ENV for tokens — they are visible in docker history and image metadata
Limitation: cache mounts are not shared across CI runners unless you export the cache (--cache-to / --cache-from, type=registry or gha)

chapters.title: Final Images: Alpine vs Distroless vs Scratch
points: The final stage decides what ships: pick the smallest base that still runs your binary
scratch: an empty image, ~0 MB, for fully static binaries (Go with CGO_ENABLED=0)
alpine: ~5–8 MB, uses musl libc and busybox, has a shell and apk package manager
distroless (gcr.io/distroless/static, base, nodejs, java): no shell, no package manager, only runtime and CA certs
debian-slim: ~30–75 MB, glibc, widest compatibility, easy debugging
Size comparison for a Go service: golang:1.22 ~800 MB, debian-slim ~85 MB, alpine ~15 MB, distroless/static ~8 MB, scratch ~6 MB
Alpine gotcha: musl differs from glibc — some Python wheels and Node native addons fail or must compile from source
Distroless has no shell, so docker exec -it sh fails; use the :debug tag or docker debug / ephemeral containers
scratch has no CA certificates, no /etc/passwd and no timezone data — copy them from the builder stage
Example: COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ for HTTPS calls from scratch
Security: fewer packages means fewer CVEs in scanners like Trivy or Grype and a smaller attack surface
Mistake: choosing alpine for a glibc-linked binary built elsewhere — fails with 'not found' at exec time

chapters.title: --target: Dev, Test and Prod Stages
points: docker build --target test . builds only up to and including the named stage
One Dockerfile can hold base, deps, dev, test, build and prod stages
Common graph: base → deps → (dev | test | build) → prod, with prod copying from build
dev stage: adds hot-reload tooling and devDependencies, CMD ["npm","run","dev"], used with bind mounts
test stage: FROM build AS test then RUN npm test — a failing test fails the docker build
CI pattern: docker build --target test . then docker build --target prod -t app:1.0 .
With BuildKit, stages not required by the target are skipped entirely
docker-compose: build: { context: ., target: dev } selects the stage per environment
If no --target is given the last stage in the file is built, so keep prod last
Output-only stages: docker build --target export --output type=local,dest=./out . extracts files without an image
Mistake: putting a dev stage last so a plain docker build ships dev tooling to production
Mistake: a typo in --target gives 'target stage could not be found'

chapters.title: ARG and ENV Across Stages
points: ARG is a build-time variable set with --build-arg NAME=value; ENV persists into the running container
An ARG declared before the first FROM is global but usable only in FROM lines
To use it inside a stage, redeclare it there: ARG VERSION with no value inherits the global default
ARG scope ends at the stage boundary — each stage must declare the ARGs it needs
Example: ARG GO_VERSION=1.22 / FROM golang:${GO_VERSION} AS build / FROM alpine:${ALPINE_VERSION}
ENV values also do not cross stages unless the stage is built FROM the earlier stage
Predefined build ARGs: TARGETOS, TARGETARCH, TARGETPLATFORM, BUILDPLATFORM for multi-arch builds
Cross-compile pattern: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang AS build then GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build
ARG changes invalidate the cache for later instructions that use it
ARG values show in docker history, so never pass secrets through them
Promote an ARG to runtime with ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION
Mistake: using an ARG inside a stage without redeclaring it, so the value is empty

chapters.title: Non-Root Users and Hardening
points: Containers run as root (UID 0) by default, so an escape or bug has maximum privilege
USER instruction switches the user for later RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT
Create the user in the build stage: RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S -G app app (alpine) or useradd -r (debian)
Numeric UID is safer for Kubernetes runAsNonRoot checks: USER 10001:10001
Distroless ships a ready user: gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot runs as UID 65532
scratch needs a hand-made /etc/passwd copied from the builder stage
COPY --chown=app:app ensures files are readable by the runtime user
Ports below 1024 need root unless capabilities are added; use 8080 instead of 80
Read-only root filesystem: docker run --read-only with tmpfs for /tmp complements non-root
HEALTHCHECK needs curl or a shell on alpine; for distroless use a built-in binary subcommand
Mistake: placing USER before a RUN that needs root, such as apk add, which then fails
Mistake: writable app directories owned by root so the non-root process cannot write logs or temp files

chapters.title: .dockerignore and Cheatsheet
points: .dockerignore lists paths excluded from the build context sent to the daemon
Smaller context means faster builds and fewer accidental cache busts from irrelevant file changes
Typical entries: .git, node_modules, dist, *.log, .env, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, coverage
Syntax: glob patterns, ** matches any depth, ! re-includes an exception such as !README.md
Ignoring .env and credentials keeps secrets out of COPY . . layers
Without it, COPY . . copies a host node_modules over the container's, breaking native modules
Per-Dockerfile ignore: Dockerfile.prod.dockerignore beside Dockerfile.prod (BuildKit)
Mistake: ignoring a file your Dockerfile COPYs, causing 'file not found' during build
Cheatsheet: FROM x AS s | COPY --from=s | --target s | RUN --mount=type=cache | ARG redeclare | USER nonroot
Checklist: pin base tags or digests, order layers by change rate, cache mounts, minimal final base, non-root, .dockerignore, test stage in CI
Summary: build fat, ship thin — keep toolchains in builder stages and copy only artifacts into a small non-root final image
